speechtext:

For many Albertans and many of the 60,000 people expected to migrate into Alberta next year, there will be waiting lists for apartments, doubling and tripling up, illegal or below standard shelter, or people being forced to leave because they cannot find shelter.

subsubtopic: WRITS OF ASSISTANCE-REQUEST FOR ABOLITION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Justice who has responsibility at law with respect to writs of assistance. The minister knows that writs of assistance provide the holder with extraordinary legal ability to carry out searches and seizures without search warrants. There is no discretion provided to the court with respect to issuance, no back-up material need be

December 2, 1981
Oral Questions
filed outlining the reason for issuance, and there is no time limit imposed upon the duration of these writs.
As the Minister of Justice will know, the Solicitor General has been putting out floaters with respect to the lifting of the moratorium imposed by the minister's predecessor, the Hon. Ron Basford. The Solicitor General has put out other floaters with respect to the prosecution of Nazi war criminals in Canada, which has now been repudiated by the Minister of Justice.
The Minister of Justice has now had an opportunity to consider his position and the position of the government in this matter. I wonder whether the minister will stand in his place and make an unequivocal declaration that the moratorium on writs of assistance will not be lifted and, indeed, that writs of assistance will be abolished by the government.
[ Translation]

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Justice and Minister of State for Social Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister of State for Social Development
subsubtopic: WRITS OF ASSISTANCE-REQUEST FOR ABOLITION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, yesterday I had an opportunity to appear before the committee, and I said that the moratorium imposed in 1977 by my predecessor, Mr. Basford, was still in place and that for the time being, we had no intention of making any changes.

Madam Speaker, the Minister of Justice knows that today is the day on which we will be voting on the constitutional package, which involves a Charter of Rights and Freedoms. As the minister well knows, that Charter contains the principle that the individual in Canada should be free from unreasonable search and seizure, yet he stands in his place and supports the continuation of writs of assistance. By not repudiating the Solicitor General the Minister of Justice is allowing the Solicitor General to make policy for the government by default.
In view of the fact that today is the day to demonstrate that there is bona fide on the part of the government with respect to civil liberties, I want to ask the minister once more to accept his responsibility and repudiate, once and for all, these lifetime licences to break and enter the homes of Canadians.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Justice and Minister of State for Social Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I said that the moratorium is still in place, and I do not intend to change that. When the RCMP appeared in committee, it was explained to the members that there are circumstances when police officers are on duty in which they need some instrument to be able to discharge their responsibility. The number of writs has now been reduced to eighty, and we would like to see further reduction. I repeat that we do not intend to change the moratorium, but I do think at one point we will have to look at alternative mechanisms to help the police discharge their responsibility and at the same time make sure that the rights of Canadians are well protected.

Madam Speaker, what the minister suggests would be quite all right, but when questioned in the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs Commissioner Simmonds of the RCMP indicated that writs of assistance would not be the cure in connection with the drug problem in Canada. The minister's assumptions are indeed wrong in this particular instance.
The minister also knows that the Law Reform Commission, which reports to him, is undertaking a study on the efficacy of writs of assistance. A report on that study will be released in April of next year.
All I want the minister to tell me is who in fact is in control of this matter. Will the minister stand and indicate that the Solicitor General will be building the policy in this matter? Is it the policy of the government to allow ministers to go around the country, at great expense, promoting their own particular fetishes and ideas respecting policy? Possibly in the case of the Minister of Finance he might have done some good in that respect, but is the Minister of Justice going to allow the Solicitor General to keep promoting this, and will the minister stand mute while this policy comes into effect by default?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Justice and Minister of State for Social Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: Madam Speaker, after the small speech of the hon. member I do not have to add anything. I stated the policy of the government very clearly. The moratorium is still in place. We are concerned about the problems of the RCMP in discharging their responsibility. At the same time we are concerned about the need of Canadians to have their rights protected. I think the situation is well in hand at this time, and if there is some change I will announce it to the House of Commons.

subsubtopic: CLEAN UP OF OIL SPILL IN ARCTIC WATERS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport. Yesterday the Canadian Arctic Resources Committee released a study that documented how it took the federal government nine months to handle an oil spill from the vessel Edgar Jourdain at Hall Beach in the Arctic, involving something like 20,000 gallons of diesel fuel. Given that the study established in great detail that the government's response to this oil spill was characterized by "bureaucratic indecision, interdepartmental wrangling and an unwillingness to act", will the minister admit that the Edgar Jourdain incident demonstrates beyond any doubt that the government is incapable of handling any kind of oil spill, whether major or minor, especially in Arctic waters?

subsubtopic: CLEAN UP OF OIL SPILL IN ARCTIC WATERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, that is not the information I have. My information is that the Edgar Jourdain was grounded in September, 1980,
December 2, 1981

and that burn-off operations were carried out in June, 1981. The public hearing was held in April, 1981. I have questioned my officials on this subject. They explained to me that the burning-off operation could not be conducted because of the weather. Consequently, they had to wait until spring to do it. With respect to the hearing, there is nothing abnormal in the time it took to set it up. I was told that throughout, local government, industry, all the interested parties, were kept fully aware of what was happening.

Madam Speaker, the minister should go back to the drawing board. He should certainly go to a different group of officials and get the real facts, including the fact that it took the Department of the Environment six weeks to respond to a request from the owners of the vessel Edgar Jourdain for guidance in disposing of the petroleum on board that vessel. In view of the minister's confusion and the fact that there is a conflict between what officials of his department are saying and what environmentalists and conservationists are saying, will he support a full inquiry into the Edgar Jourdain incident with a view to preventing a similar disaster and a similar shambles in the future? Will be at least admit the need for an inquiry to look into the whole matter?

Madam Speaker, I want to emphasize that public hearings were held on this matter in April, 1981. The hon. member is doing his job and I will do mine. Now that he asks me to look into the matter further, I will, and report to him very rapidly.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT MEASURES BE INTRODUCED TO CURB EXCESS PROFITS
REQUEST THAT MEASURES BE INTRODUCED TO CURB EXCESS PROFITS
speechtext: This is my final supplementary to the Prime Minister. I wish he would just try to take an interest in problems that really do concern the average Canadian and that hit the average Canadian where it really hurts. Given the fact that Governor Bouey was quick to defend the chartered banks' profits, which have been at record levels as announced just in the last two or three days-50 per cent for the Royal Bank, 40 per cent for the Toronto-Dominion Bank, profits in the hundreds of millions of dollars-and given the fact that the budget has clearly failed to address the central economic questions facing the country, why will the Prime Minister not introduce additional measures to the budget which will deal with the problem of excess profits, which will deal with the problem of the economy in a recession, and which will provide some hope for Canadians facing the most difficult winter in 25 years?

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR AID FROM GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. It has become more than evident that last month's budget, which the minister supported, is having a devastating effect on small business and most other sectors of our economy. While the
government's excuse is fiscal restraint, yesterday the minister dipped into funds made available through the Industry and Labour Adjustment Program to buy off his already disenchanted home town of Windsor with a $6 million interest free loan, in order to help Hilton Hotels expand their chain to his city. Could the minister justify this action when he knows full well that $6 million interest-free would create more full-time jobs in small business, for example? When will the government stop catering to large multinationals and start helping the small guys?

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR AID FROM GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR AID FROM GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Industry and Labour Adjustment Program is designed to help create new long-term viable employment in the communities designated under it. It permits assistance to eligible commercial activity which makes sense in the community. subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF FUNDS FOR HIGHWAY RESEARCH
speechtext:
1.	In the past five years, what amount was allocated by the government to highway research and science?
2.	Does the government presently maintain research facilities to research highway technology and, if so, what are the facilities?
3.	From 1976 to 1980, what amount went toward research of urban transportation?
4.	Since 1970, did the government commit funds to provincial or municipal governments for building an urban transportation system and, if so, in what amount?

speakeroldname: Mr. David Smith (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF FUNDS FOR HIGHWAY RESEARCH
speechtext:
I am informed by the Departments of Public Works, Regional Economic Expansion, Supply and Services and Transport as follows:
1.	The Transportation Development Centre of Transport Canada (TDC) in the past five years has allocated approximately $200,000 to highway research and science.
The Department of Public Works also made a contribution of $50,000 in 1976 to the Ontario ministry of transportation and communications to aid in developing a better code for the design of highway bridges. In addition, $84,000 was allotted in the last five years for contracts to study bridge vibration and thermal and construction stresses, and $20,000 was contributed to two studies under contract by Department of Supply and Services.
The Department of Supply and Services through its unsolicited proposal program contracted for the following three studies:
(i)	Study of transverse distribution of vehicle loads on highway bridges, $30,000 DSS and $10,000 DPW.
(ii)	Analysis and design of box bridges and voided slab bridges, $49,950 DSS.
(iii)	Study of the effectiveness of intermediate diaphrams in distributing five loads in beam and slab bridges, $18,000 DSS and $10,000 DPW.
2.	TDC does not maintain research facilities to research highway technology.
3.	From Fiscal years 1976/77 to 1980/81 TDC spent approximately $10,250,000 toward research of urban transportation.
4.	The TDC has since 1970 often cost-shared R & D projects with provinces and/or municipalities on R & D projects to improve components of various urban transportation systems. The costs of these R & D projects are included in the amount described in part 3 above.
Through the Transport Canada Urban Transportation Assistance Program, established in 1978, approximately $47.4 million has been approved for urban transportation projects of various sorts and $97.5 million has been approved for the construction of railway grade separations.
Since 1970, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion committed a total of $167,689,071 in grants and $20,037,111 in loans to provincial and municipal governments for building of urban transportation systems.

speechtext:
In so far as the Department of Communications is concerned, the reply to the above question is as follows:
1.	The Government Telecommunications Agency requires certain information for billing and planning purposes on calls made by the use of government call codes. The information, which is entered on mark sense cards by government operators consists of: point of termination, point of origin, called number, call code number, and connect and disconnect times. This data is provided only on written request to authorized officials of departments or agencies to which the call codes have been specifically assigned. subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, when I last spoke to the House about Bill C-48 it was on November 10, and the government did not see fit to continue with this bill until now. It was obviously not very important to the government. Frankly, we would prefer the government not to proceed any further with this bill. It contains some of the worst legislation ever to come before this House.
I had related to the House the effect this measure was having on small business in Canada. I also related that members of the NDP and the Liberal Party stated how concerned they were about small business in Canada. This legislation affects small business and how small business relates to the oil industry. Over the past year many small oil companies have shut down. Many have left for the United States and Australia. Many have gone out of business. All of this is because of the efforts of this government to nationalize the oil industry.
I also related to the House how numerous members from the other side said that we would have energy self-sufficiency by 1990. I mentioned that in 1974 the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said that we would have oil self-sufficiency in 1980. He said that from 1974 right through to 1980, but we do not have it at this time. Now he says we will have energy self-sufficiency by 1990. This is the same Prime Minister who in 1974 said they had beaten inflation. We all know that inflation has not been beaten.
The Independent Petroleum Association, the Canadian Petroleum Association and the National Energy Board all say that we will not have oil self-sufficiency by 1990, but this socialist Liberal government says we will.
We presently consume 1.8 million barrels a day and produce 1.4 million barrels a day, resulting in a shortfall of 400,000 barrels daily. According to the latest figures, by 1990 our production will be down by 700,000 barrels a day. The government has no means at the present time to recover that shortfall. Technology is not in place to do this and the government knows it. The government will admit this but not in public. They say they will put the technology in place to do that. How can we do that and at the same time allow the oil rigs to leave the country?
We do not have the technology on the east coast, in the Beaufort Sea or in the Arctic, the three areas affected by this bill. All the oil companies are prepared to say is that they are working on it. They worked for ten years in the North Sea to bring in those wells. This government says that within the next few years it will bring in the wells in the Arctic, on the east coast offshore and the Beaufort Sea.
Yesterday representatives of the Independent Petroleum Association appeared before the Senate banking committee. They reported that approximately 256 rigs are drilling in Canada at present, 150 rigs are idle, 180 have left Canada, 34 are under construction and will leave Canada. Of the 620 rigs in Canada, only 256 are drilling.
The ratio of rigs to wells drilled in Canada in one year is approximately 20 to 1. The government is telling us that we are going to drill between 6,000 and 7,000 wells this year compared to the 10,000 which the oil companies and drilling companies told us we could drill in 1981. This is all due to the Canadianization program which the government has backed us into.
We call this program of Canadianization confiscation. Members opposite have repeatedly stood and said that this only pertains to the oil industry. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. MacLaren) stood in this House and related the special place
December 2, 1981

which the oil industry has in Canada. He said that Bill C-48, which provides for a degree of government involvement in frontier lands, lands that belong to all Canadians, represents a pragmatic response to a particular set of circumstances.
Last weekend one of the Liberal hit men, Jim Coutts, called for Canadianization of other industries such as mining, forestry, farm machinery, telecommunications and the auto industry. They have been hiding behind this. We have known for a year that this is what they intend to do. All one had to do was talk to members of the staff of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. They will admit privately that it is nationalization, not Canadianization. To go further, last weekend the Minister of Communications (Mr. Fox) urged the government to adopt a national cultural policy similar to the national energy policy, even though the national energy policy has supposedly been shut out with the new energy agreement. However, we know it has just been changed.
On November 3 in a statement in this House, the parliamentary secretary glossed over some of these provisions. He said that the rule prior to 1977 was that if you drilled on any federal lands, you had to give back to the Crown 50 per cent of those lands and they would in turn put them up for bid once again. That was changed in 1977. Those were terrible conditions and the government was going to improve the situation, allowing a person to keep all the lands on which he drilled. The government said it would waive the royalties. In exchange for that, it asked for 25 per cent ownership in everything that is drilled. In other words, a Canadian company or the government must own 25 per cent of all wells drilled.
Along came Hibernia. Where was the government? Canadian companies did not want to get involved, so they approached Petro-Canada. Petro-Canada did not want to get involved in Hibernia, but because of the legislation it had no choice. It was forced to come in-fortunately, hopefully, for Canada in the future. This field will end up to be a very exceptional one in terms of oil fields in Canada.
From 1977 to the present day the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources skipped over it completely. He never even mentioned this back-in clause of Petro-Canada, this supposedly 25 per cent Canadianization. He glossed over it entirely and stated that they were going from a 50 per cent ratio of Canadian ownership to what we have at the present time, a 25 per cent back-in clause, or confiscation. He does not even know half of what is in this bill, but he is quite prepared to read a statement prepared by the department. That is what he has done in the house most of the time: he is quite prepared to read statements that the department prepare for him. He does not even know the legislation that is in effect at the present time.
With this bill the government says that we will have self-sufficiency by 1990. Where is it? It is certainly not there in their actions. It is certainly not evident in the budget that was just provided. As everyone is aware, the 1980 budget was really a national energy policy that was bootlegged into the House.
Canada Oil and Gas Act
The 1981 budget has done nothing more than take the heat off the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) and transferred the burden to the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). Surely most hon. members in the House assumed that the Minister of Finance was too smart to get caught in this bind.
We need to look no further, Mr. Speaker, than at what happened in Toronto last weekend when 1,500 Liberals met to talk about how they would turn this country into a socialist state. And a socialist state they do intend. We have no self-sufficiency plan for Canada. All we have is a housing industry that is falling apart, a forest industry in B.C. that is in desperate straits, a fishing industry on the east coast where 50 per cent of the fishermen are unemployed. Is this the government that will provide benefits for Canada? Will it provide an energy policy that will solve the problems of Canada when it cannot even solve the other problems? It is almost ridiculous the way this Liberal government goes on and on assuming that the Canadian people will keep voting for them because they will give them something around election time.
Many hon. members on the other side will not see this House after the next election. In fact, one can almost start to say goodbye to most of them now. So many of them will not return to this House that if one were to say goodbye to each one of them, it would take a long time.
Certainly many members on the other side are pretty concerned about their seats at the present time because a few people, without consultation with industry, without consultation with the provincial governments, have introduced a bill which will not provide self-sufficiency for this country.
They talk about Canadianization. This back-in clause is nothing but confiscation, Mr. Speaker. I should like to refer, in particular, to one clause, I believe it is Clause 38. Can one believe that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, who heads up PetroCan, is also the arbitrator of any disputes? So if PetroCan and an oil company, in partnership, have a disagreement, then according to the provisions of Clause 38 the matter shall be submitted for arbitration in the manner provided for by order of the Minister. In other words, the minister will decide the means of arbitration and then the minister will arbitrate. Not only that, but when he does arbitrate, under Clause 38 his decision is final and binding on all affected parties. What a ridiculous bill!
As one further studies this bill it gets worse. At times I do feel sorry for some of the members opposite who are prepared to vote for such terrible legislation; they have allowed themselves to become so degraded that they are more interested in the patronage which the Liberal Party has given them oyer the years and when it tells them that if they vote with the party they will receive more patronage in the future. Unbelievable!
Many hon. members on the other side call themselves Liberals, but this bill is just another rubber stamp on the socialist policies that we have had for 13 years. There are not many members on the other side who are prepared to stand up and call a spade a spade, but that is what it is-socialism. Socialism is the key word for the next election. Do we want

December 2, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
socialism under these members opposite or do we want free enterprise? Do we believe that the individual is supreme or do we believe that the state is supreme?
These socialists on the other side are not building a system or a better Canada; they are tearing it down. How can one say that they are building a better Canada when they put people out of work? Is there any member on the opposite side who is prepared to say that this energy policy is creating more jobs? I ask them to stand up and tell me how many jobs have been created in Alberta in the last year. Tell me how many jobs have been lost in Alberta over the last year? Thousands of them. What member on the other side is prepared to say that not one job has been lost in Alberta over the last year? Stand up now. We have silence, Mr. Speaker, because they are all mutes over there. They are not prepared to stand up on that point.

speechtext:
Certainly it is interesting when a backbencher of the Liberal Party rises to say that we are speaking on amendments. We are speaking on the bill. All the amendments have clearly been dealt with.
For a moment I should like to discuss history. We should recognize that Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba at one time were all part of the so-called massive Canada lands, as is the case with the Northwest Territories. At one point they were just territories. When Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba were brought into confederation, they did not have ownership and control of their natural resources. Indeed, there was a rape of the industrial, mineral and resource bases of those provinces until 1930 when the central or controlling provinces clearly recognized that they must give control of natural resources to Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba so that they would be treated in exactly the same manner as any other province in confederation. Clearly members of the government are not learning from the people of the Northwest Territories and Yukon. They are not treating the people who were born and raised in the north, or those who moved to the north, with any degree of foresight. They are robbing those people of their heritage. It is as much their heritage as the heritage of people born in Quebec, in Newfoundland or in Alberta. The problem has not been addressed. It astounds me when I think about it.
All regulatory control of resource development will be the direct responsibility of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. In some minor cases it will be the responsibility of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro). There is a clear conflict. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources does not have to account to the people or the governments of the Northwest Territories or Yukon. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, where it is applicable, does not have to account to the governments of the people of the Northwest Territories or Yukon. A very serious mistake is being made by allowing Bill C-48 to proceed in its present form. Virtually the people of Yukon and Northwest Territories are being told, "Forget it, you will never have the wherewithal to become a province".
If one has travelled extensively in Canada and in the north, one will realize that a number of things stand out about the people of those areas-their individuality, their strength and their determination to develop the territories in exactly the
December 2, 1981

same manner that the founding people of Quebec, Ontario and Alberta established their provinces, those immigrants from other parts of the world and those people from other parts of Canada who established and hued out those provinces. The people of the north are exactly the same kind of people. They are still pioneers and they are proud of it. With Bill C-48 they are being told to forget it because the mighty czar of energy, mines and resources will control what goes on in the Northwest Territories and in Yukon, the so-called Canada lands. Also they are virtually being told that they will never be able to carve out a province as did the founders of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia.
One cannot consider Bill C-48 without talking about aboriginal rights. Effectively it eliminates aboriginal rights in many ways. It undermines the negotiations and the commitment of the federal government. It clearly undermines aboriginal and native rights in the north. If the government is clearly interested in native people in the north, it should come to grips with the problems there; this should be done now. They should make settlements prior to development and prior to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources moving in with the discretionary powers that are outlined in this bill.
There is a debt here that has not been paid, Mr. Speaker, and that will become evident when development begins. The signals are there already. The people of the north, the Dene people, the aboriginal people, the Indian people, are not going to allow the uninterrupted development of the natural resources in the territories until they know that they will be treated fairly by the government. That is a warning that we should heed, Mr. Speaker.
Bill C-48 gives very wide discretionary powers to the minister. In committee discussions I put forward what I thought was a logical argument but it fell on deaf ears. I suppose it will fall on deaf ears again today. The minister has wide discretionary powers to decide what oil company, what private consortium, what public consortium, is going to be able to develop this or that area and who is going to get this or that lease. If a find is made, the minister may determine how big that find is. He may say that he wants three more wells to be drilled. The private company that has sunk the hole and found reserves could be at odds with that and say that the find does not justify three wells and would not be commercially viable. The minister could overrule the company and say, "You will drill three more wells; if you do not, we will take the lease away from you." That is the kind of discretionary power the minister has.
I do not think that these are the kind of powers the minister wants. I have not seen any legislation that has passed this House in the short time that I have been here which opens the door to such abuse. There is the opportunity for pork-barrelling, for favouritism, for nailing someone you do not like. The minister has put himself in the position of Solomon and clearly, Mr. Speaker, he is not Solomon.
Canada Oil and Gas Act
Bill C-48 has an enormous impact on Canada, not just on the gas and oil industry alone. The enormity of the program was recognized by the minister when he introduced the national energy policy and said that the decisions relate to energy but that they will impinge on almost every sphere of Canadian activity, on every Canadian and on the economic and social structure of the country for years to come. He also said that they would have major and positive implications for the federation itself. I would ask my colleagues to examine that statement and try to digest it in the context of Bill C-48.
I agree with the minister that Bill C-48 has that kind of implication. We are either going to develop into a country with individual initiative, individual thought and the individual gamble that will be rewarded, or else we are going to develop into a country that will cater to the mediocre. We will develop into a nation of enterprise, of individual initiative, or else-and Bill C-48 is a clear indication of this-we will develop along the lines of a socialist state.
During the debate that culminated in the House today, we on this side wanted a very small provision put into the Constitution of Canada, and that is the basic right to own property. The Liberals refused, however. A study of Bill C-48 indicates why they refused. Of course, they were spurred on by their socialist friends in the corner, the little red rump. But at least the people in the corner are honest; they tell us exactly where they stand. They are for government ownership and for socialism-for the mediocre. They say that constantly so at least we know their views. We do not hear that kind of statement from the Liberal benches, however, because they disguise their views, but that is what has happened.
The whole thing is designed so that preferential treatment will be given to the Crown corporation. No compensation is provided for the initiative of an entrepreneur who goes out and finds oil, but there is a 25 per cent back-in provision. That will only pay immediate costs. There are laws in this country that deal with expropriation. Certainly governments can expropriate property, but compensation is paid and there is recourse to the court of appeal. Although there is some provision in Bill C-48 for compensation, there is no appeal provided.
I have already mentioned the discretionary powers of the minister and they scare me, Mr. Speaker. A great deal of time and money has been spent in putting a staff together that has the necessary expertise to develop an oil property. An instance of this is the Hibernia play. No single company could afford to go out to the Hibernia and drill a well offshore. No one company could stand the risk involved and so a consortium was formed.
As many as 22 companies could be involved in a consortium which was drilling only one well. Each company could take as little as one half of 1 per cent of the action or 10 per cent of it, depending upon how much they can risk. But together, the companies determine who will be the over-all operator. They may select Dome because of its experience in the Beaufort Sea, or they may select Petro-Canada as the company having the most knowledge.

December 2, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
Under this legislation however, that will no longer be the case. The minister may determine at any time, with any consortium with which Petro-Canada is involved, who shall be the operator. It does not matter if Petro-Canada has only 1 per cent of the action. The minister may make a determination and say to a company: "You are going to allow Petro-Canada to be the operator." A great deal of time, effort and expense is involved to put the staff with the necessary background and expertise together. It will be absolutely devastating if the operator were removed for political reasons. But that is what we are giving the minister the power to do. Clearly if you do not like the way the operator is running the project, it is the consortium that sits down and says: "We do not want you there. We do not think you are doing it the way the majority of us would like you to do it; therefore, you will be removed." That is not the case with Bill C-48. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and his senior bureaucrats, the mandarins, can determine who is going to be the operator of the consortium if Petro-Canada is part of it. That is total and absolute abuse.
There are national and international implications to Bill C-48. Clearly we have not looked at them. We have not examined the stability of our legislative framework. Clearly we have not looked at the protection of personal property rights. Clearly we have not looked at the sanctity of a contract. But these very things are absolutely necessary if we are to gain a degree of stability in our investment climate in the eyes of our national and international business community. We need investment in this country. But no one will invest in this country, no one from outside Canada will invest, and many in Canada will not invest in their own country without the protection of property rights. People will not invest in Canada if we do not have a legislative framework that gives us stability.
Canada has always through its courts strongly defended property and contractual rights. Canada has been known worldwide as being a safe climate in which to invest because individual rights were protected, corporate rights were protected and property rights were protected. The provisions of this bill violate every one of those concepts.
I urge hon. members across the way to think through this bill very clearly and I ask them once and for all to sit down and read it. I urge them to look at the implications for the people in the Northwest Territories and Yukon, the implications for the native people, the aboriginals and the Dene. But more than that, I tell members across the way to look at what this bill is telling the rest of the financial community in the western world. This bill is telling the financial community very clearly not to invest in Canada because we do not protect property rights and individual rights, nor do we have a legislative framework giving stability. We confiscate in Canada as they do in banana republics. That is what we are saying by passing this bill, so I urge hon. members to think it through clearly.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it may not be an accident that we are discussing this particular bill immediately after the House has just expressed itself on a question of grave and fundamental importance, that of a change in our Constitution.
My hon. friend and colleague who just preceded me made some references to the fact that one should read Bill C-48 if one is to understand some aspects of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms which now, at least in the House of Commons, has been entrenched in the Constitution. It may not be an accident because there were certain aspects of this Charter of Rights and Freedoms which gave me and some of my colleagues from all sides of the House serious and dramatic difficulties, and may I just touch on one.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, one of the major objectives of Bill C-48 is energy self-sufficiency by 1990. What that means is not only massive and costly exploration and development efforts in Canada lands, but massive amounts of money, incalculable amounts. Some say between $300 billion to $500 billion is required to carry this out. Naturally, when one embarks on that kind of effort, knowing the incredible risks involved and the chances that have to be taken to develop new oil, one also knows that little things, such as environmental and human concerns, cannot stand in the way once the bulldozers move into a promising area.
Let me touch on one issue. I shall compare this with what happened in Quebec when that province decided to move with almost indecent haste to develop the James Bay power potential. There were certain environmental concerns that had to be considered. They were quickly bridged, but the people created more of a problem. Most of the people there were native people. Some had to be moved to another area. Some of them were unwilling to go, but there was no time to negotiate. Therefore, some kind of a settlement was legislated. We talked with the native people. We asked them what they wanted. They did not like the price. The native people were told that while the negotiations were going on the bulldozers had to operate. As we know, the native people sought refuge in the courts and obtained an injunction to stop the work. Work on the James Bay development was shot down until an accommodation and a settlement were reached, a settlement of the legitimate rights and a price for which the native people of James Bay asked.
I want to return to the Constitution. We entrenched certain native rights in the Constitution today. They were not the same rights that were in the resolution that emerged from the parliamentary committee, that great exercise that was displayed to all Canadians throughout our country for months on end. That resolution said that native rights should be respected, recognized and affirmed. While it was not perfect, it was a step in the right direction. As you know, sir, the way we have been treating our native peoples in this country is a national disgrace, and it has earned us the condemnation of other countries and of international tribunals. We are being looked at almost like South Africa in the way it is treating its native peoples.
December 2, 1981

The resolution that came before the House and is now entrenched in the Constitution had a word added to it, and that word is "existing". In other words, only the rights which now exist are recognized and affirmed. It does not matter how many times the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) says this word really does not mean anything. First of all, he is intellectually dishonest in saying that, in that legislators, particularly the Minister of Justice, are not supposed to be writing words into fundamental laws that have no meaning, unless they are wantonly and deliberately trying to confound the courts. We are not supposed to be writing words into the Constitution that have no meaning. No, the Minister of Justice knows what the word "existing" means and why it was written in.
If we were to apply the new charter with respect to the rights of the native people in the James Bay situation at the time they went to the courts to seek refuge and obtain an injunction, the judges would have had no other way to interpret their demands than to say: "You have no existing rights; your rights have not been established and do not exist, so how can we grant you an injunction on the basis of something you do not have? We have a clear indication from Parliament, from the Premiers of all the provinces, and we assume there will be ratification by the government of the United Kingdom, that the only rights you have are rights that now exist." We know what would have happened. The work would not have been stopped, a settlement would have been legislated and, undoubtedly, it would have been something much less than what the James Bay people finally achieved for themselves.
It may not be an accident because there are other things in this Constitution and some aspects of this charter of rights that are more important because of omissions rather than because of things that are written; for instance, the omission of property rights, which my colleague touched on.
Property rights relate to the right to own and enjoy property, which is the very basis, foundation and beginning of western civilization. It is now a secondary kind of right, it is no longer a fundamental right. It would have been very difficult to do what the minister or his agent, PetroCan, is doing in relation to the Canada lands, if we had written in the Constitution one of the main features of the Diefenbaker bill of rights, and that is the right to the ownership and enjoyment of property, because the companies in the north who have now had their property confiscated would probably have been able to make a claim in the courts on the grounds of the Constitution. Naturally, that is no longer so. The statement my colleague made that members should read Bill C-48 if they are worried about the ominous consequences of what we have done here today is probably quite right.
I have said that the basic principles and objectives of Bill C-48 are laudable enough, and they are two. The first is a greater degree of Canadian ownership. I personally would not like to put a percentage figure on that, but certainly 50 per cent is a reasonable objective, particularly since we had already achieved that Canadian ownership content before we began with Bill C-48. Of course, I have to qualify that by
Canada Oil and Gas Act
saying that that includes all the energy play and not just drilling, the companies actions and the service sector, which was mainly owned by Canadian companies.
The other component principle or objective is self-sufficiency. Naturally that has to be a main objective, and it is certainly one that my party has pursued very actively with great energy and vigour.
Let us talk about Canadian ownership for a moment. We all know that we have to generate and assemble the kind of capital required to carry out what is necessary to be done in ten years. Not only will we have to find 400,000 barrels a day of new oil by the year 1990, but we have to replace almost one million barrels a day of oil that is now coming from the conventional shallow reserves in Alberta, which in the main will have been depleted by the year 1990. New oil will have to be found to replace that.
We all knew that in order to assemble the necessary capital to carry out these massive exploration and development schemes, the price of energy would have to rise. All of us agreed it simply did not make sense that we should sit in an energy-poor world and charge for our own resources within our own country a fraction of what it was worth in the international world. We also knew that if we were to go closer to the world price, if we were to double the price of gasoline and heating oil, someone in the energy sector, particularly the oil companies, would be making excessive profits-their profits would not be reasonable in relation to the cost of production and the other factors involved.
The oil companies all expected us to bring in a measure that would protect the Canadian consumer and give the companies a direction on how their profits would have to be reinvested. They fully expected that royalties and economic rent would be adjusted so that the government could either tax or charge away through economic rent some of those profits which would have been in excess of a reasonable profit reflecting costs of production.
The oil companies thought the government already had all the tools necessary to do that without confiscating their assets and without actually entering the energy sector itself. We could have adjusted our economic rents, as we do with any other natural resource sector. In the lumber sector, which I know most about, the provincial governments adjust their stumpage rates to reflect the world price of lumber. Whenever the price goes up, stumpage goes up; whenever it goes down, stumpage goes down. Right now in British Columbia, at least, stumpage is at a bare minimum. The companies pay very little for the resource they are taking from the public domain.
The oil companies expected that to happen, but they also knew this could have been done another way. There could have been guidelines and directions on how oil companies' excess profits should be reinvested; in other words, they could not pay them out in dividends, and they could not take them out of the country. We could have said that excess profits have to be put back into development and exploration.

December 2, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
Further to that, the oil companies fully expected that the government would tell them where to explore and develop. This has to happen on Canada lands and they cannot go anywhere where the government does not make proper leases available to them. The government knew that it had all the tools necessary to protect Canadian interests in the energy sector, but it did not choose any of these conventional tools because, to the draftsmen of this bill, Canadian ownership meant government ownership.
I would like to talk for a moment about the way Bill C-48 was drafted. I served on the committee which received this bill for consideration. It contains 85 clauses and it became quite clear, even in the early stages of committee discussion-even before it went to committee-that as soon as the government let it be known what it was about to do, it became quite obvious what some of the consequences of this action would be. Naturally, we came to committee prepared and armed with certain amendments and proposals that we thought would improve the measure and at least restore a degree of confidence that was lost in our ability to manage our resources.
It was an incredible situation and I do not know if there is any precedent for it, but we were told in committee that the government would not accept any opposition amendments of any kind. At the same time, however, the government laid before the committee no less than 115 amendments of its own, none of which redressed some of the more serious aspects of the bill which has now led our energy sector into a serious situation.
The bill was actually drafted by this committee. The bureaucrats were there, sitting around and saying, "If you do not like this, we will move another amendment." There were 115 amendments introduced by the government to approve a bill which should never have come before the committee in the first place. It was obvious that the term "Canadian ownership" meant government ownership and that Petro-Canada was to become an agent of the minister, not to participate in the energy play on Canada lands, but to take over control. Canada lands were identified as our northern territories, the Yukon, the offshore and certain other regions. Petro-Canada was given 25 per cent of every lease in operation on Canada lands.
My colleagues have spoken on this aspect and pointed out that, because of the incredible risks often associated with some of the major development plays in the north, particularly the risks associated with developing new technology, it has been a tradition with the oil companies that whenever the risks get high they seek to share them with their partners in the industry.
For example, we do not yet know how we will bring oil ashore from the Beaufort Sea and how we will protect the infrastructure under the ice pack from scouring and so on. Nor do we know how we will bring Hibernia oil ashore and transport it to the marketplace. That has still to be developed and there are serious risks involved.
Well, these oil companies have a partner now. It is called the governor in council and its agent, Petro-Canada, who will own 25 per cent outright. In most cases, even if it states that Petro-Canada will own 25 per cent, which is not entirely assured, if a company is still below Canadian ownership content of 50 per cent, Petro-Canada will confiscate the rest. But even if it is only 25 per cent, in most cases Petro-Canada will be the major shareholder in the larger plays.
Earlier in the debate I said that we have not yet considered the incredible risks and contingent liability that the minister has placed on the backs of the taxpayers of Canada as a result of this particular action. We are going to be the major players and the major risk-takers in the oil patch. By "we" I am referring the Canadian taxpayers. If it costs approximately $400 billion between now and 1990, it will cost the Canadian taxpayer $100 billion to pay his share in the energy play on Canada lands.
Many people are confused about why our interest rates are so high when at the same time we have such a high rate of inflation. It has never been a mystery to me. When a government is out in the marketplace trying to raise large amounts of capital and pay 2 per cent or 3 per cent above market rates of interest, it is no wonder that interest rates are high. When a government maintains a $13 billion or $14 billion deficit and then goes into the marketplace to borrow money to pay last year's interest, there is no doubt that interest rates will stay high.
Interest rates are one of the key factors of inflation because a businessman who cannot pass his costs of doing business on to the consumer will not stay in business very long. That is why we have both high inflation and high interest rates. It is something which has never been written into the textbooks. That is why economists are shaking their heads in utter disbelief; they do not have a solution to the situation because Adam Smith, Friedman and Galbraith did not write it into the textbooks. They have never had to deal with a government like ours, which taxes the poor and fundamentally changes the way it should behave in the marketplace.
The government is spending $3 billion alone to buy up private companies and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) says that that is only a beginning. He has not yet actually spent $3 billion because he does not have it, but he has accepted a liability of $3 billion to purchase these two oil companies, which were doing quite well, were producing quite a lot of oil, although they were more active in the retail market than they were in the exploration and development field.
The government does not just want to be sure we are energy self-sufficient by 1990, it also wants to be sure that the Canadian taxpayer has a share in the corner service station. It is incredible to think that the government would go to Petrofina and say that it would like to buy their oil company but that it does not have the money. It told them: "Our credit is good, though, and New York will lend us the money, but we do not want to go to the taxpayers, and tell them what we are about to do and to increase the deficit even further, because

that is such a public thing. What we want is for you to carry the credit."
We are yet to be told, Mr. Speaker, what interest rates the minister has committed us to when he made the Petrofina deal. All we know is that this Belgian company is no longer owner of a Canadian oil company, but it is holding $1.5 billion of Canadian credit. If it were possible to imagine anything like that, it would boggle the mind to consider that that situation

will continue until 1990 and that that is the kind of liability which the minister is placing on the backs of Canadians.
I see our servant is reaching for the mace, so may I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
